metadata.title: Five Steps, One Answer.
metadata.purpose: A viewer with no physics or coding background can name the engine's five steps (parse, retrieve, plan, solve, verify), say what each does to one real problem, and explain why only the first step uses a language model.
metadata.register: Explainer for newcomers — every term defined on first use
metadata.audience: Students and general viewers; no math, AI, or programming knowledge assumed.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer — the ask lands answered
beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on the five steps the physics engine takes to solve a problem. We'll follow one problem all the way through. A car starts from rest and speeds up at two point five meters per second squared, for twelve seconds. How fast is it going, and how far did it travel?

props.command: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2.5 m/s² for 12 s. How does the physics engine find its final speed and distance?
output: Only the first step uses a language model
Answer: 30 m/s and 180 m, checked two ways

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, the five steps, in order: parse, retrieve, plan, solve, and verify. Second, what happens to our car problem at each step, including the one step where an A.I. model is allowed to help. And third, what comes out the other end. Not just a number, but a record of how it was found. No physics or coding background needed.

The answer up front. Each step has one job. Parse reads the problem. Retrieve finds formulas that might help. Plan checks whether the problem can actually be solved with what's given. Solve does the math. Verify checks the answer. Only the first step uses a language model. The other four follow fixed rules, so once the problem is read, the same input always takes the same path.

beats.new_visual_element: the sentence becomes knowns, each with its phrase
beats.narration_text: Step one, parse. The model reads the sentence and writes down what's known and what's asked. Acceleration, two point five. Time, twelve. And starts from rest means a starting speed of zero. Every value keeps the exact phrase it came from, so a wrong number can be traced back to a misread word. The model's instructions say it must not solve anything, or compute any value.

Step two, retrieve. The engine keeps a library of formula cards, thirty-one of them in this version. Each card holds its equations, when they apply, and the common mistakes. Retrieve pulls every card that can solve for what we asked: a speed, or a distance. Six cards qualify, from springs to satellites to waves. Retrieve deliberately doesn't check yet whether we have enough information. That's the next step's job.

beats.new_visual_element: closure check — five gaps, one closes
beats.narration_text: Step three, plan. This is the closure check. For each card: does it have every known it needs, and do its equations pin down an answer? The spring card needs a spring constant. Not given, so it's out. The other four are missing something too. Only the constant acceleration card has everything: starting speed, acceleration, and time. If no card closed, the engine would stop here, say exactly what was missing, and log the gap instead of guessing.

Step four, solve. SymPy, a symbolic math library, does the algebra. Final speed equals starting speed, plus acceleration times time. Zero plus two point five times twelve: thirty meters per second. Distance equals half of acceleration, times time squared. Half of two point five, times one hundred forty-four: one hundred eighty meters. No number is typed in by hand. Every value comes from the solver.

Step five, verify. First, the engine plugs the answers back into the original equations and checks that both sides match. Then, for this card, it finds the distance a different way: speed squared equals two times acceleration times distance. Thirty squared is nine hundred. Divided by five, that's one hundred eighty. Same answer, two paths. So the status is verified.

beats.new_visual_element: the solution object — a record, not just a number
beats.narration_text: What comes out isn't just thirty and one hundred eighty. It's a solution object: what was read, which card matched, why the plan closed, how it was solved, and which checks passed. So when an answer is wrong, you can see which step went wrong. And that's the takeaway. Whenever an A.I. model gives you an answer, ask what it read, which formula it used, and how it checked.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with any physics problem. It asks Claude to work in the same five steps, and to label each one.

props.command: Here is a physics problem: [paste it]. Work in five labeled steps. 1 Parse: list knowns, unknowns and units, quoting the phrase each came from. 2 Retrieve: name candidate formulas. 3 Plan: check you have every known each one needs. 4 Solve: do the math in code. 5 Verify: check the answer a second way.
output: Parse — knowns with their source phrases
Plan — what's missing, said out loud
Verify — a second path to the answer

beats.new_visual_element: title restate, terracotta period, name beneath
beats.narration_text: Parse, retrieve, plan, solve, verify. This has been Param Madan. Thanks for watching.
